blocks.content: Beyond the basic mechanics covered in the Dockerfile module, using USER correctly for security has a few practical details worth knowing: how to create the user, why a numeric ID sometimes matters, and a common permissions gotcha.

The typical shape creates a dedicated, unprivileged user earlier in the Dockerfile, then switches to it with USER before the final CMD, so every layer needing elevated permissions (installing packages, for instance) still runs as root, while the application itself never does.

blocks.alt: Create the user, then switch to it before the app runs

blocks.content:
RUN adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" appuser
COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . /app
USER appuser
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

code.content:

COPY --chown=appuser:appuser . /app
USER appuser
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

blocks.content: 2. Why a Numeric UID Sometimes Matters
blocks.text: 2. Why a Numeric UID Sometimes Matters

blocks.content: Minimal base images, distroless images especially, often have no /etc/passwd entries at all, referencing a username that does not exist there would fail. Using a plain numeric UID (USER 1000) sidesteps that entirely, it works whether or not the image has any user database.

blocks.alt: A numeric UID works even without a user database in the image

blocks.content: 3. Verifying Who a Container Actually Runs As
blocks.text: 3. Verifying Who a Container Actually Runs As

blocks.content: It is worth actually checking rather than assuming, docker exec with id or whoami confirms exactly which user a running container's processes are executing as, a quick, direct sanity check.

blocks.alt: A direct check, not an assumption

blocks.content:
docker exec mycontainer id
# uid=1000(appuser) gid=1000(appuser)

code.content:
docker exec mycontainer id
# uid=1000(appuser) gid=1000(appuser)

codes.bash:
docker exec mycontainer id
# uid=1000(appuser) gid=1000(appuser)

blocks.content: Files copied into the image before the USER switch are owned by root by default, if the application later tries to write to one of them as a non-root user, it fails with a permissions error. The fix is COPY --chown= (as shown above) or an explicit RUN chown before switching users.

blocks.alt: Files owned by root need an explicit chown before switching users

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: Create a dedicated user and switch to it with USER before the app runs, keeping earlier setup steps that genuinely need root separate.
A numeric UID sidesteps missing /etc/passwd entries in minimal images, and COPY --chown= avoids the classic "non-root can't write its own files" gotcha.
